chapter.title: Essential Oils and Resinoids; Perfumery, Cosmetic or Toilet Preparations

page.h1: HTS Chapter 33: Essential Oils and Resinoids; Perfumery, Cosmetic or Toilet Preparations — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: Exporting Cosmetics, Perfume & Essential Oils from the U.S.: Schedule B, EEI, FDA Certificates & Hazmat (HTS Ch. 33) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What the U.S. requires to export cosmetics, perfume, toiletries and essential oils: Schedule B numbers, EEI filing, the Russia luxury-goods licence, FDA export certificates, hazmat rules for perfume and aerosols, CITES oils, and how to pay less duty abroad.

intro: What the U.S. requires before essential oils, fragrances, cosmetics and toiletries leave the country, and the legal ways to pay less abroad. For most products the work is routine: find the Schedule B number, screen the buyer and file the export in AES. No U.S. agency must approve a cosmetic before export, but many buyers' regulators ask for an FDA export certificate, and the product itself decides the rest: alcohol-based perfumes and aerosols ship as hazardous materials, sunscreens and antiperspirants are drugs under U.S. law, oils from a few protected plants need CITES papers, and perfume and make-up need a licence for Russia and Belarus.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: Chapter 33 Schedule B numbers start with the six digits shown on the Overview: 3304.99 for skin care and sunscreen, 3303.00 for perfume and cologne, 3302.10 for flavor bases sold to food and drink makers, 3302.90 for fragrance compounds, 3304.10 for lip and 3304.20 for eye make-up, 3305.10 for shampoo, 3306.10 for toothpaste, 3307.20 for deodorants and antiperspirants, and 3301.29 for most other essential oils such as lavender or tea tree. A sunscreen or antiperspirant stays in Chapter 33 even though FDA regulates it as a drug.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Chapter 33 goods are not on the Commerce Control List, so they are EAR99 and most destinations need no licence. The exception is Russia and Belarus: fragrance compounds (3302.90), perfume (3303), make-up and skin care (3304.10–3304.99) and other toiletries (3307.90) are on the EAR 'luxury goods' list and need a licence for any value (15 CFR 746.8(a)(7), Supplement No. 5 to Part 746). Cosmetics and perfumes are also listed examples of luxury goods for North Korea.

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: Shipments to Canada, the largest buyer, need no EEI filing unless they need a licence or are moving through Canada to a third country (15 CFR 30.36). A licensed shipment of perfume or make-up to Russia or Belarus needs an EEI filing at any value.

rules.title: Cosmetics export certificate: FDA does not require one to export, but many buyers' regulators (for example the UAE's Montaji registration) ask for a certificate of free sale. FDA's version is titled "CERTIFICATE" and is requested online through the Certificate Application Process (CAP) in FDA's eCATS; FDA issues it only for products whose intended use is solely cosmetic.

citations.label: FDA: online applications for cosmetics export certificates

rules.title: Cosmetics that don't meet U.S. requirements (for example a color additive or label made for the buyer's market): exportable under FD&C Act 801(e)(1) if they meet the foreign buyer's specifications, do not conflict with the importing country's laws, are labeled on the outside of the shipping package as intended for export, and are not sold in the U.S. Keep records showing this for 3 years.

Sunscreens, antiperspirants, fluoride toothpastes and anti-dandruff shampoos are over-the-counter drugs in the U.S.: FDA will not issue a cosmetics certificate for them. Buyers who need a certificate get a Certificate of Pharmaceutical Product from CDER through CDER eCATS ($175 for the first).

Flavor bases for food and drink (3302.10) are food ingredients under U.S. law. FDA does not require a certificate to export them; when the buyer's authority asks for one, FDA issues food export certificates (such as a Certificate to a Foreign Government) through HFP eCATS.

Facility registration and product listing under the Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act cover cosmetic products distributed in the United States (21 U.S.C. 364a–364b). They are not an export step: they apply when a product is also sold in the U.S., which is usually the case for products FDA certifies for export.

citations.label: FDA: registration and listing of cosmetic product facilities and products

rules.title: Alcohol-based perfumes and colognes, and most essential oils, are Class 3 flammable liquids (UN1266 "Perfumery products with flammable solvents"); hair sprays, deodorant sprays and room sprays in aerosol cans are UN1950. The shipper must classify, pack, mark, label and document them and train its staff; small retail packs can ship as limited quantities. Air shipments also follow the IATA/ICAO dangerous-goods rules.

Essential oils and extracts from CITES-listed plants need a CITES export or re-export permit: rosewood oil (Aniba rosaeodora) and palo santo or guaiacwood oil (Bulnesia sarmientoi), except finished products such as fragrances that contain them; agarwood (oud) oil from Aquilaria and Gyrinops, except finished products packaged for retail; and spikenard (Nardostachys grandiflora). Musk from musk deer is a CITES-listed wildlife product that also needs a declaration (Form 3-177) before export.

Fragrance compounds and essential oils sold for industrial use are TSCA chemical substances; finished cosmetics are not. If a product contains, at 1% or more (0.1% for a listed carcinogen), a chemical subject to a TSCA section 4, 5, 6 or 7 action, the exporter sends EPA a section 12(b) export notice.

groups.label: Essential oils, resinoids & extracted oleoresins
groups.note: Most essential oils ship as flammable liquids; rosewood, palo santo, agarwood and spikenard oils also need CITES papers.

groups.label: Fragrance & flavor mixtures (incl. beverage flavor bases)
groups.note: Flavor bases (3302.10) are food ingredients; fragrance compounds (3302.90) sold to other manufacturers are TSCA chemical substances.

groups.label: Perfumes & toilet waters
groups.note: Alcohol-based perfumes and colognes ship as UN1266 flammable liquids. Perfume needs a licence for Russia and Belarus.

groups.label: Makeup, skin care, sunscreen & nail preparations
groups.note: Sunscreens and products with drug claims are OTC drugs, so certificates come from CDER. Make-up and skin care need a licence for Russia and Belarus.

groups.label: Hair preparations (shampoo, perms, hair spray)
groups.note: Anti-dandruff shampoos are OTC drugs; hair sprays in aerosol cans ship as UN1950.

groups.label: Oral & dental hygiene (toothpaste, floss, mouthwash)
groups.note: Fluoride toothpastes and anticavity rinses are OTC drugs.

groups.label: Shaving, deodorants, bath, room fragrance & other toiletries
groups.note: Antiperspirants are OTC drugs; aerosol deodorants and room sprays ship as UN1950.

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

savings.title: Have the Chinese buyer apply for an exclusion from China's 2019 counter-tariffs
savings.saves: China's 2019 counter-tariff on U.S. goods: 25% on perfume, make-up, hair, oral-care and other toiletries and 27.5% on skin care, leaving the normal rate plus the 10% extra.
savings.appliesTo: Chapter 33 goods of U.S. origin imported into China; almost every line is on China's 2019 counter-tariff lists.
savings.document: The Chinese importer applies through the State Council Tariff Commission's market-based exclusion process; the U.S. exporter supplies the contract and product details.
savings.caveat: Exclusions are valid only until December 31, 2026 unless China extends them, and they do not remove the 10% extra duty on all U.S. goods.

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
